turn.subject: diagnosis
turn.user_message: Revenue per bed is about ₹32,000. Most patients are fit by 10 and leave around 3, so roughly 5 hours. The doctors usually decide who’s going on the 7 PM round — they just don’t sign till morning.

text: Your real problem isn’t slow discharge. It’s unused time, and nobody owning it.
Let me explain. Your doctors already decide in the evening. But nothing moves until the morning round ends, and most of the discharge work could be done in that gap. Nobody uses it today because:
bullets: There’s no automation, so starting early means doing the work twice.
Nothing is coordinated until the doctor signs.
No one has ever been asked to use the evening.
chat.invite: The second cause is ownership: your own numbers put you past both lines where discharge needs one owner. Does this match what you see on the wards?
chat.note: The time is already there — nobody uses it.

points.label: Nobody owns discharge end to end

prompts: Yes — show me what fixing it looks like

blocks.title: Unused time, and no one owning it
blocks.deck: Two causes behind the wait — both visible in your own answers.

blocks.caption: A ceiling: holds only if each freed bed is filled again the same day.

items.title: About 16 unused hours
items.text: Doctors decide at 7 PM. Nothing moves until the 11 AM round.
items.more: Half the discharge steps — draft summary, provisional bill, insurance pre-approval, pharmacy returns, family briefing — could start in that window. Today none do, because starting early means doing the work twice.

items.title: Nobody owns discharge
items.text: Each team finishes its step. No one owns the whole wait.
items.more: Delays get blamed on ‘the process’. At your volume, coordination is the bottleneck, not effort — and coordination needs an owner.
